```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(agecraft)
```

Sometimes a whole-number age is all you need. For example, a report might
ask only for completed years at enrollment. Other analyses need more: distinguishing
a newborn from an older infant, carrying units through a workflow, or applying
the same named groups consistently across several tables.

agecraft provides two complementary S3 classes for these tasks:

| Class | What one element represents | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `age` | A numeric age in a specified unit | 2.75 years |
| `age_group` | A right-open interval in a specified unit | From 1 up to 3 years |

Both classes use the vctrs framework to support vector operations. `age_group`
also builds on the ivs interval framework. You can use them as columns in an
ordinary data frame without learning their internal implementation.

## One sample data frame

We will follow the same fictional observations throughout this guide. Each row
has a participant identifier, a birth date, and a visit date. One birth date is
missing so we can see how missing observations behave.

```{r sample-data}
visits <- data.frame(
  id = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"),
  birth_date = as.Date(c("2025-06-20", "2025-01-01", "2023-01-01",
                         "2021-01-01", "2010-01-01", "1980-01-01", NA)),
  visit_date = rep(as.Date("2025-07-01"), 7)
)
visits
```

These fixed dates make the examples reproducible. Keep the original dates when
you can: they let you recalculate ages in another unit without approximating a
conversion from years or months.

## The age class

### Why keep an age object?

An `age` vector stores fractional numeric values and **one unit for the entire
vector**. Its default display shows completed whole units. That combination lets
you present familiar ages while keeping precision for classification.

For a simple completed-year report, this is enough:

```{r plain-completed-ages}
visits$completed_years <- calculate_age(visits$birth_date, visits$visit_date,
                                        unit = "year", output = "numeric")
visits[c("id", "completed_years")]
```

However, both a newborn and an older infant have zero completed years. Use an
`age` vector when you need to preserve that difference:

```{r calculate-age-column}
visits$age_years <- calculate_age(visits$birth_date, visits$visit_date,
                                 unit = "year")
visits[c("id", "completed_years", "age_years")]
is_age(visits$age_years)
attr(visits$age_years, "unit")
```

The two columns may look similar when printed, but only `age_years` retains
fractions and its unit. Missing birth dates produce missing ages without
removing the corresponding row.

### Stored values versus displayed values

Compare three ways of looking at the same column:

```{r inspect-age-values}
visits$age_years
format(visits$age_years, fractional = TRUE)
as.numeric(visits$age_years)
as.integer(visits$age_years)
```

`format()` changes the representation; it does not modify the values.
`as.numeric()` removes the class and unit and returns full fractional values.
`as.integer()` extracts completed whole units. It is truncation, not rounding
to the nearest birthday.

That differs from `calculate_age(output = "numeric")`, which calculates and
returns completed ages directly. The third output choice,
`calculate_age(output = "units")`, returns completed ages as a units-package
vector. Choose `output = "age"` (the default) when you want to keep fractions.

### How fractional ages are calculated

For years, `calculate_age()` adds the fraction of civil days between the previous
and next birthdays to the number of completed birthdays. A leap birthday reaches
its next year on March 1 in a non-leap year. For months, it uses consecutive
calendar month anniversaries, rolling back to the last day of a shorter month.
Both boundaries are calculated from the original birth date to avoid drift.

For POSIXct inputs, years and months use civil dates in the starting time zone
and ignore time of day. Smaller units use elapsed time: days are 24 hours and
weeks are seven such days. A daylight-saving transition can therefore result
in a fractional elapsed day.

### Construct or convert age objects

When ages have already been calculated elsewhere, construct a vector from the
numbers and their known unit:

```{r construct-age}
reconstructed <- age(as.numeric(visits$age_years), unit = "year")
reconstructed
```

`age()` constructs from plain numeric values. `as_age()` converts plain numbers,
existing age vectors, or suitable time-units vectors:

```{r convert-to-age}
converted <- as_age(as.numeric(visits$age_years), unit = "year")
is_age(converted)

unit_values <- units::set_units(as.numeric(visits$age_years), "year")
as_age(unit_values)
```

Supply the correct unit: these functions cannot infer whether a bare number
means years or days. Negative and infinite ages are rejected; missing ages are
allowed. Wrapping a completed-year number in `age()` cannot recover the
fraction that was previously discarded.

### Select, sort, summarize, and combine

The age class stays attached during ordinary vector operations:

```{r age-vector-operations}
visits$age_years[1:3]
sort(visits$age_years, na.last = TRUE)
c(visits$age_years[1:3], visits$age_years[4:7])

average_age <- mean(visits$age_years, na.rm = TRUE)
average_age
as.numeric(average_age)
```

Comparison uses fractional values, not their completed-unit display:

```{r compare-ages}
visits[which(visits$age_years < age(1, unit = "year")), c("id", "age_years")]
```

Age vectors must have matching units when you combine or compare them. Means,
extrema, and rounding retain the class. General arithmetic and transformations
such as logarithms are deliberately unsupported. If an analysis needs plain
numbers, explicitly extract them with `as.numeric()` and keep their unit clear
in the surrounding code.

### Convert to another unit

Use `as_age()` for explicit unit conversion. The conversion factors come from
the units package. Fine-unit conversions, such as days to weeks, use fixed
ratios. To demonstrate that with our participants, first calculate elapsed days
from their original dates:

```{r exact-days-and-weeks}
visits$age_days <- calculate_age(visits$birth_date, visits$visit_date, unit = "day")
visits$age_weeks <- as_age(visits$age_days, unit = "week")
visits[c("id", "age_days", "age_weeks")]
```

The fractional part of `age_weeks` is a fraction of a week. The fractional part
of an age in days is a fraction of a day.

Converting **years or months to days** is approximate because calendar years
and months vary in length. The conversion uses unit conversion factors, not
an individual's birth date. You must opt in to this approximation:

```{r approximate-days}
visits$approximate_days <- as_age(visits$age_years, unit = "day",
                                  allow_approx = TRUE)
data.frame(id = visits$id,
           days_from_dates = as.numeric(visits$age_days),
           days_from_years = as.numeric(visits$approximate_days))
```

The two numeric columns can differ. If exact elapsed days matter, calculate
in days directly from the dates. Setting `allow_approx = TRUE` acknowledges
the approximation; it does not make the conversion calendar-exact.

### Age function reference

| Function or operation | Use |
|:--|:--|
| `calculate_age(start, end, unit)` | Calculate an age vector from dates |
| `age(x, unit)` | Construct from numeric values |
| `as_age(x, unit, allow_approx)` | Convert values or change units explicitly |
| `is_age(x)` | Check whether a vector has the age class |
| `format(x, fractional = TRUE)` | Display the stored fractions |
| `as.numeric(x)` | Extract fractional numeric values |
| `as.integer(x)` | Extract completed whole units |

## The age_group class

### Why represent groups as intervals?

A text label such as `"Toddler"` does not tell R where that category begins or
ends. An `age_group` vector stores the interval boundaries separately from its
optional name. Classification can use the boundaries while tables display the
name.

Each interval includes its lower boundary and excludes its upper boundary.
For example, `[1, 3)` contains ages beginning at the first birthday and ending
just before the third birthday. Its ordinary completed-age label is `1-2`.
For completed ages 1 through 3, use `[1, 4)`.

### Construct groups from bounds

Define a set of categories for the same sample data. The boundaries and names
below illustrate the mechanics; choose definitions appropriate to your analysis.

```{r construct-groups}
groups <- age_group(start = c(0, 0.077, 1, 3, 13, 20),
                    end = c(0.077, 1, 3, 13, 20, Inf), unit = "year")
groups
is.age_group(groups)
```

Fractional boundaries are preserved without rounding. Only upper boundaries
may be infinite. The unit is shared by the whole group vector. A unit of `NULL`
means the unit is unspecified; it does not mean different elements have
individual units.

The first cutoff, `0.077` years, approximates 28 days. For an exact 28-day
boundary, define groups in days and classify `visits$age_days` instead.

### Convert existing definitions

`as.age_group()` accepts numeric cut points, supported completed-age labels,
factors of those labels, or ivs intervals. For example, the same sample can
also be classified using the package's five-year preset:

```{r supplied-definitions}
preset_groups <- as.age_group(age_group_presets$Yr.5, unit = "year")
head(preset_groups)
categorize_age(visits$age_years, by = preset_groups)
```

The supplied definitions are numeric cut points; specify their intended unit
when constructing the group vector. Confirm that a preset fits the reporting
conventions of your analysis.

For custom numeric cuts, a final `Inf` creates an open-ended final group.
A final finite cut also creates a final one-unit interval in `as.age_group()`;
use `age_group(start, end)` when you want to control every upper bound explicitly.

### Name the groups

Assign names in the same order as the intervals:

```{r name-groups}
names(groups) <- c("Neonate", "Infant", "Toddler", "Child", "Teen", "Adult")
data.frame(category = names(groups),
           lower = ivs::iv_start(groups), upper = ivs::iv_end(groups),
           unit = attr(groups, "unit"))
```

Names describe the categories. `as.character(groups)` continues to describe
the boundaries, and `format(groups)` also shows the unit. Names do not change
interval equality or chronological ordering.

```{r describe-groups}
as.character(groups)
format(groups)
```

### Classify the sample and carry names into a table

```{r classify-sample}
visits$category <- categorize_age(visits$age_years, by = groups)
visits[c("id", "age_years", "category")]
is.ordered(visits$category)
levels(visits$category)
table(visits$category, useNA = "ifany")
```

The result is an ordered factor, with levels in interval order. The category
names become its labels and therefore the labels in `table()`. Classification
uses full fractional ages: the newborn and older infant both display as
`0 year`, but enter different categories.

Unnamed groups use interval labels. Missing or blank names fall back to
interval labels, and distinct intervals must have unique resulting labels.
Missing ages and ages outside every interval return `NA`.

### Keep intervals instead of factor labels

If a later step needs interval boundaries rather than a category factor, ask
for interval output:

```{r keep-intervals}
visits$matched_group <- categorize_age(visits$age_years, by = groups,
                                      output = "interval")
visits$matched_group
names(visits$matched_group)
```

This returns one matched `age_group` per observation, preserving repeated
assignments, missing observations, units, and category names. A factor alone
does not retain structured interval boundaries.

### Select, combine, and compare groups

```{r group-operations}
groups[1:3]
names(groups[1:3])
sort(groups[c(3, 1, 2)])
vctrs::vec_c(groups[1:3], groups[4:6])
generics::as.ordered(groups)
```

Names follow the intervals through selection, sorting, and concatenation.
Combining group vectors requires matching units, including whether a unit
is specified. Trying to change an existing group unit with `as.age_group()` is rejected:
relabeling the numeric bounds would not convert them.

`compare_age_groups()` can inspect widths and relationships between interval
vectors. For example:

```{r group-widths}
compare_age_groups(groups, operation = "width")
```

Widths are measured in the group's coordinate unit: a width in years is not
an exact elapsed-day duration. The function also supports crosswalks,
membership, ordering, age-gap bounds, and interval set operations. Set operations
can merge or split intervals, so they discard category names. See
`?compare_age_groups` for those more advanced operations.

### Keep matching rules explicit

For simple one-category-per-person reporting, use non-overlapping groups.
The package allows gaps and overlaps; `categorize_age()` raises an error if
an observation matches more than one interval by default. Its `multiple`
argument can choose the first or last match in sorted interval order when
that is the intended rule.

When ages and groups have different specified units, `convert_units` controls
which side is converted. Conversions between fine units and months/years require `allow_approx = TRUE`.
For the sample workflow we avoid that approximation by calculating ages in
years for year-based groups, or in days for day-based groups. Groups without
a specified unit are interpreted in the age vector's unit; unitless numeric
ages with explicitly unit-bearing groups are rejected.

### Age-group function reference

| Function or operation | Use |
|:--|:--|
| `age_group(start, end, unit)` | Define explicit interval boundaries |
| `as.age_group(x, unit)` | Convert cuts, labels, factors, or intervals |
| `is.age_group(x)` | Check whether a vector has the age_group class |
| `names(x) <- labels` | Assign category names |
| `categorize_age(ages, by = groups)` | Return an ordered category factor |
| `categorize_age(..., output = "interval")` | Return matched intervals |
| `age_cat_iv(age, age_group)` | Alternative interval classification interface |
| `generics::as.factor(x)` / `generics::as.ordered(x)` | Convert groups to factors using names |
| `compare_age_groups(x, ...)` | Inspect interval relationships and widths |

The sample data frame now contains the original dates, precise ages in explicit
units, and named categories. Keep the precise age column for classification and
analysis, and choose a completed-age display or extraction when that is what
your report needs.
